Review Body:
At least deserved the one star for being a relatively quick read for an almost 300 page book, but that's the only positive thing I can say. Really didn't resonate with me at all. Too much blatant embellishment, cliche wisdom, and ego to take anything of value away from this book.

Other reviews mention the casual dismissal of legitimate child abuse being swept under the rug because "oh hey I turned out fine, and my dad and mom were cool most of the time, so it was all love"; as a kid with no building experience somehow building a towering thirteen story treehouse 100 feet high all by himself; him following his wet dreams across the world as if they were supernatural revelations; his father passing away as he climaxes having sex with his mom, etc. that all contribute to Mcconaughey coming off as someone who enjoys telling a few too many tall tales and lacks the awareness that he's even doing it. Overall he seems just a bit too full of himself for my liking.

A small, random example I just read, that would've made me put down the book if I wasn't 30ish pages from the end: As a footnote, when referring to an interview with MTV where he was discussing his acting come back and taking on more serious roles, Mcconaughey tells us "Did you know I made up, coined, and created the term McConaissance? I did." Then only a few sentences later in that same footnote he quotes himself in that interview "I actually did an interview the other day and THE JOURNALIST called it (his career revival) a 'McConaissance'." So 1) It was a strange flex to begin with, and 2) you didn't actually make up, coin, or create "McConaissance" - a journalist from a previous interview did.

Not too long after that, when discussing a family get together he says "we catch up with each other, drink, eat, and tell lies." Just casually dropping that telling lies is a common family trait apparently. If the book hadn't constantly knocked me over the head with far fetch story after far fetch story throughout I probably wouldn't have even noticed, but when I find myself nitpicking instead of just reading that's when I know a book isn't for me. It's little things like that littered throughout that make it hard to believe/care about anything that's written.

It's always possible I just wasn't in the right mood when I read this, but I think reading Mcconaughey's Wikipedia and Googling "cool bumper sticker slogans" would've given me the same amount of joy and saved me some time.

Review Body:
I bought Greenlights just under 40 hours ago, it was on sale and I had the chance to get it for free on Audible. I have since listened to all 6 hours and 51 minutes, binging it in multi-hour sessions while I drove through the night. A review convinced me to bite the bullet on the audiobook, after saying that it felt like McConaughey was sharing his life through a passionate and insightful phone call, rather than a detailed memoir, and I am inclined to agree.

McConaughey goes into detail about his hardships in life; How he learned to grow and change for the betterment of himself. He talks in-depth about taking advantage of the negatives and turning them into positives; rather than fighting with the provocations of his life, learning to challenge them & using those experiences to better himself and solidify his values. I saw a lot of myself and my own struggles throughout the read, and I have ultimately taken a lot away from the wisdom and undaunting passion that he details on the path to finding himself, and bringing himself to become the person that he is today.

It's an inspiring read, and whether you find that you can relate to it or otherwise, I can confidently say that it is worth the time spent on every word. Every red light is bound to turn green, and every passage that closes, every opportunity that may stand in your path, will not only lead to a green light, but that particular series of red, yellow, and green lights are ultimately what makes your story your own. These are the values that Greenlights encapsulates, and these are the values that make this story so much more than your standard celebrity memoir. No matter if you love Matthew McConaughey, or you're an active reader, looking for a good autobiography, this book is the perfect read, and I cannot recommend it enough. Words do not do it justice.

Review Body:
In "Greenlights," Matthew McConaughey shares an introspective and candid look at his life, filled with the wisdom he's gleaned over fifty years. Drawing from over three decades of personal diaries, McConaughey combines anecdotes, insights, and reflections that paint a picture of his experiences, triumphs, and struggles. The result is not just a memoir but a guide to navigating life's complex riddle.

The book’s central theme revolves around the idea of "catching greenlights," which symbolizes moments of success and flow that come when one understands how to manage life's inevitable challenges. McConaughey's style is refreshingly relatable, as he shares stories that range from the humorous to the profound, illustrating lessons about love, loss, and the pursuit of authenticity. With a mix of anecdotes, poetry, and even some personal affirmations and beliefs, he crafts a narrative that encourages readers to embrace life’s ebbs and flows with grace and humor.

"Greenlights" is more than a Hollywood memoir; it's an exploration of what it means to live fully and intentionally. McConaughey's genuine reflections, paired with his unique perspective, offer readers a welcome dose of inspiration and a reminder that, much like traffic signals, life’s challenges can eventually lead to green lights. This heartfelt love letter to life serves as a delightful mix of wisdom, humor, and motivation, making it a rewarding read for anyone seeking to catch more greenlights in their own journey.
